palette: deep emerald green tile against white and chrome
topic: brushing one wall and leaving the rest of the photo untouched
angle: Masking Studio changes the region you paint and nothing else. Everything outside the brush is the original photograph rather than a re-render that happens to look similar, which is the claim a whole-photo tool cannot make.
visualSummary: A two slide deep blue field. Both slides carry the same photograph of a bathroom at the same crop, marked with four numbered pins in identical positions and a numbered legend beneath. The room is a white freestanding bath against a large square tiled wall, a chrome floor standing tap rising beside it, two rolled grey towels on the rim, a window throwing daylight from the left and a pale tiled floor. Slide one is the original: the wall is plain off white ceramic. Slide two is the same frame after one brushed edit, the wall now deep emerald green on the same tile grid, the green running edge to edge and around the tap. The bath, the tap, the towels, the window, the daylight and the floor are pixel identical between the two slides. Deep emerald green and white against the blue chrome.

copy.headline: One wall changed.
copy.caption:
We brushed one wall. The bath, the tap and the towels are the same pixels they were before.

That is the whole of Masking Studio. You paint over the part you want changed, and everything outside the brush is left exactly as it was. Not re-rendered, not redrawn. The original file.

The alternative is restaging the whole photo, and that gives you a new room rather than a new wall. The bath moves. The tap grows a second handle. The light from the window lands somewhere else. It all looks fine until you put it next to the picture you started with.

So here is the check. Swipe back and forth and watch the chrome on the tap, the fold in the towels, the shadow the bath casts on the floor. Nothing moves.

We measured it rather than trusting it: of the 185,295 pixels outside the brushed area, zero changed.

One photo. One brush. One pass.

Save this for the next time a client asks what a different tile would look like.

Virtually staged with Stagify.ai

images.note: Generated rather than stock, and not for want of trying: thirty photographs across ten stock queries were screened and every one was rejected, because a real bathroom almost always has a mirror, a vanity or a glass screen crossing its main tiled wall. This post needs one broad uninterrupted wall, since the model will retile a large area cleanly and declines to retile a narrow strip. This is the SAME bytes the edit started from, taken from the pipeline rather than resized to match by hand, and cropped by the SAME rectangle as the after frame.

generation.prompt: Remove the existing pale ceramic wall tile and replace every part of it with deep emerald green glazed ceramic tile. Large plain square tiles with a smooth flat surface, thin pale grout lines, the same tile grid and the same perspective as now.

defects: The green tile is not fully saturated and has a gradient across the wall.
quality.authorNote:
Two things in this record were nearly shipped wrong, and both were invisible to every automated signal available at the time.

First the colour. An earlier prompt asked for 'sea glass green, a muted grey green' and the model delivered the muted grey with no green at all, moving the wall by deltaE 0.40 across its lower half, which no eye can see. quality.perfect was true, bestScore was 100, and a pixel diff said 98 per cent of the brushed area had changed, because a one-value shift counts as a change. The deltaE bands recorded above exist because of that, and they are the only measurement here that speaks to whether a viewer can SEE the edit rather than whether it happened.

Second the fine horizontal lines that covered the finished tile. They survived four prompts, three mask geometries, five seeds and both image models, and they were in none of those: the model's raw output was clean the whole time. sharp promotes a raw single-channel buffer to sRGB across a blur, so the feathered composite mask came back with three channels where the code indexed one, and reading the interleaved bytes as single channel left every third row of the mask fully transparent. The original white wall showed through one row in three. The fix is one call and a length assertion in mask.js; the cost was most of a day.
